strand_a.title: The nuclear-climate nexus for net-zero pathways: Opportunities, challenges, and policy directions: A review
strand_a.summary: Although solar, wind, storage, efficiency and electrification remain essential for net-zero pathways, many power systems also require firm low-carbon resources, resilient infrastructure and governance arrangements that can sustain reliable energy services under extreme weather, geopolitical disruption and growing industrial demand. This review therefore develops the Nuclear-Climate Nexus as a system-level framework for evaluating nuclear energy not simply as a low-operational-emission technology, but as a conditional contributor to climate mitigation, adaptation, energy security and sustainable development. To address the need for validation beyond conceptual framing, this review also tests the framework against country-level and regional evidence from the United States, Korea, Canada/Ontario, the European Union and China.

strand_a.summary: ABSTRACT Highly concentrated imports can be a source of vulnerability to external shocks, especially in an environment characterized by geopolitical tensions and a potential weaponization of supply chains. strand_a.title: Government as a Strategic Actor: A Framework for Assessing Regulatory Risk in Digital Markets
strand_a.summary: This paper argues that effective risk assessment requires moving beyond a static view of government as a rule‐maker to analyzing it as a dynamic, strategic actor. We develop a tripartite framework that enables managers to evaluate regulatory risk by analyzing a state's discursive commitments (public narratives and policy signals), institutional capacity (administrative design and enforcement power), and material leverage (control over key technological infrastructure). Applied to the landmark European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the framework reveals critical “orchestration gaps” between a state's regulatory ambitions and its infrastructural dependencies.

strand_a.title: Key Policy Lessons for More Sustainable Agri‐food Trade from TRADE4SD and MATS Horizon 2020 projects
strand_a.summary: If EU policymakers want to credibly defend ‘values’ (EU standards) in the contested agri‐food trade arena, it is time to move forward collaboratively and substantively as has been achieved by both the Mercosur and India free trade agreements. Key policy conclusions are: support local contexts in markets exporting to the EU through institutional, investment and technical assistance for cooperative capacity‐building (multi‐stakeholder) and standards alignment that accounts for compliance costs differences; inclusive and robust trade governance needs investment into actor empowerment as part of capacity‐building; redesign trade agreements for closer SDG alignment through institutionalised sustainability impact assessments with a systems perspective; increase policy coherence through coordinated, predictable and impact‐assessment‐based policy instrument implementation (SDG‐proofing) and reform. The integrated methods approach highlights the need for comprehensive policy responses that acknowledge the interconnectedness of domestic, EU and international factors for achieving more sustainable agricultural trade.

strand_a.title: Cold War 2.0 and defence readiness
strand_a.summary: By quantifying the cost of unpreparedness, we provide an evidence-based rationale for European allies to embark on a gradual de-risking of trade trajectory rather than waiting for a much more costly “abrupt shock” trigger dictated by strategic challengers. As a worst case, we investigate the trade channel of geo-economic fragmentation in a Cold War 2.0 implying a complete cessation of trade with CRINK and a full blockade of Taiwan in an international multi-sectoral macroeconomic model featuring the defence sector and interlinking countries via global supply chains. In the context of simultaneous rise of external threats through CRINK and the reprioritisation of transatlantic ally’s global posture, we study how a protracted low intensity conflict with CRINK would affect European allies’ preparedness to protect the security of the citizens and the integrity of the territory.

dynamic_shocks.title: A partner weaponises Europe's dependence on critical infrastructure and networks to extract concessions
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on critical infrastructure and networks. Separate primary evidence shows that economic coercion can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of critical infrastructure and networks.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for economic coercion.
Primary evidence contains 1 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
1 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
3 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on critical infrastructure and networks for current or planned work.
Economic coercion reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: The trigger is not yet backed by an official primary source in the retained current evidence.
Only one primary retained record currently links the European capability directly to the outside pressure.
The primary direct connection is concentrated in one source, so independent confirmation is still weak.
The primary corpus contains 2 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Screen ownership and vendors of critical infrastructure early.
Build redundancy and repair capacity for cables, ports and grids.
Make the anti-coercion response credible and fast, and coordinate it with partners.
watch_for: A partner links trade measures to a political dispute.
The Commission opens an anti-coercion examination.
